reading.title: Discussing rights and legal standards
reading.text: At an adult civics seminar, Sam compares freedom of speech with the right to privacy. The facilitator explains that rights have legal contexts and lawful limits; a slogan does not resolve a dispute. Due process concerns fair procedures, and equal protection concerns unjustified unequal treatment. The right to vote, freedom of religion, right to counsel and right to assembly address different activities. The right to petition concerns asking public authorities to address a matter, while a fair trial concerns impartial proceedings. Liability means legal responsibility, and negligence concerns failure to exercise required care. The facilitator distinguishes jurisdiction, a court's authority, from precedent, an earlier decision, and statute, enacted legislation. Sam asks which jurisdiction the examples describe before drawing conclusions.

reading.title: Separating stages in a case
reading.text: The facilitator uses a fictional case to separate legal stages. A local ordinance and an official regulation set requirements; compliance means following them, while enforcement concerns making them effective. Adjudication is the process of deciding a legal matter. An arrest places a person in custody, and a charge is an accusation rather than a conviction. Bail concerns conditions for release while a case is pending. A plea is the person's formal response to a charge. A conviction is a finding of guilt; an acquittal is a finding of not guilty. Parole and probation involve supervision under different circumstances. A sentence is punishment imposed after conviction, and an appeal requests review. Specific processes depend on the jurisdiction, so the fictional sequence is not universal legal advice.

reading.title: Reading international protection terms
reading.text: Sam reads an educational overview of international relations. A treaty is an agreement between states, and convention can name a formal international agreement. Sovereignty concerns a state's authority, while diplomacy concerns relations managed through discussion. Sanctions are restrictions or penalties, not praise or approval in this context. Extradition concerns transferring a person to another jurisdiction under legal arrangements. Asylum concerns protection sought or granted, whereas refugee describes a person meeting relevant protection criteria; the terms are not interchangeable descriptions of any traveler. Human rights belong to people as human beings. The Geneva Convention label refers to treaties protecting people during armed conflict. Sam compares the meanings without deciding whether a particular person qualifies for protection or what a treaty requires in a real case.
